\chapter{But, Twice Over}
\label{ch:pa-but-twice-over}
\hlchaptermodality{39}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can set one thing against another with either word for but, and choose between a Sanskritic word and a Perso-Arabic one knowing what the choice tells my listener.}

Punjabi has two words for but, one inherited and one Arabic by way of Persian, and that pair is the same shape as the dhanvaad / shukriya pair this book taught in chapter 1 and never explained. The doublet lesson closes a point the inventory said one lesson would close. The writing lesson carries the caution the inventory needed: par is also the first two letters of parivar, which is why the corpus search returned hits and no occurrences.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[par]{\pa{ਪਰ} (par) — but}

\label{lesson:PA-C39-par}



\begin{quote}
From the chapter behind you: the word that joins two sentences, and the pattern that refuses two things at once.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{ate}, and \emph{nā … nā …}
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} joins two clauses the way \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}} does, and warns that the second will pull against the first:

\begin{quote}
\emph{(first sentence)} \textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} \emph{(second sentence)} — \textquotedblleft{}… \textbf{but} …\textquotedblright{}
\end{quote}

It works best with the chapter before it, because the sharpest contrast a beginner can draw is between something that is and something that \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}}.

\textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} is the \textbf{inherited} word — it came down with the language rather than being borrowed into it. That matters more than it usually would, because the next lesson is a second word for \emph{but} that arrived from somewhere else entirely, and this book already teaches one such pair without saying so.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Build:} two clauses joined with \emph{par}, the second negative.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} the same two clauses with \emph{ate}, then with \emph{par}.
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{par} alone, and hear how short it is.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Set one thing against another. What does \textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} warn you about the second clause? (It will pull against the first.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lekin]{\pa{ਲੇਕਿਨ} (lekin) — but, again}

\label{lesson:PA-C39-lekin}



\begin{quote}
One lesson back, the word that sets one clause against another.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{par}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{mainū̃ samajh nahī̃ āī} — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਲੇਕਿਨ}} — \emph{lekin} — \textbf{but}
\end{quote}

The same job, the same position, and a completely different history. \textbf{\pa{ਲੇਕਿਨ}} is Arabic \textbf{lākin}, carried into Punjabi through Persian — the road that also brought this book several of its greetings and farewells.

So Punjabi has two words for \emph{but}: one that grew here and one that arrived. You can use either. They are not in competition and neither is more correct.

What they are is a \textbf{pair}, and this book has been quietly teaching you another one since its first chapter without ever pointing at it. The next lesson but one is about that.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{par}, then \emph{lekin}. Same sentence, either word.
  \item \emph{Build:} a contrast, said twice, once with each.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} their lengths — one syllable against three.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give a contrast twice, once with each word. Which of the two came into Punjabi from outside, and by what route? (\textbf{\pa{ਲੇਕਿਨ}} — Arabic, through Persian.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[par]{\pa{ਪਰ} reaches the page}

\label{lesson:PA-C39-par-write}



\begin{quote}
One chapter back you wrote \textbf{\pa{ਅਤੇ}}. Write it once from memory.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{Script — two signs, and a caution worth more than the signs}
\begin{quote}
\textbf{\pa{ਪ}} — \emph{pa} · \textbf{\pa{ਰ}} — \emph{ra}
\end{quote}

Both old, and the word is two letters long. The caution is the real lesson.

\textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} are also the first two letters of \textbf{\pa{ਪਰਿਵਾਰ}}, \emph{family}, which this book taught many chapters ago. So when you meet these two signs on a page, check that they stand \textbf{alone} — inside a longer word they are not this word at all.

That is not a hypothetical. It is the reason a search of this corpus for \emph{but} came back with hits and no actual occurrences.

\subsection*{Writing — guided copy, model in view}
Copy \textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} once with the model in view. Then write it again with a space on either side, standing between two clauses, which is where it belongs.

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How do you tell the \emph{but} \textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} from the same two signs inside a longer word? (It stands alone, between two clauses.)

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \textbf{\pa{ਨਹੀਂ}} written — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[dhannavād / shukrīā]{The pair rule — \pa{ਧੰਨਵਾਦ} and \pa{ਸ਼ੁਕਰੀਆ}}

\label{lesson:PA-C39-doublet}



\begin{quote}
From the very first chapter of this book, the two ways to say \textbf{thank you}. And from two lessons back, the two ways to say \textbf{but}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{dhannavād}, \emph{shukrīā} — then \emph{par}, \emph{lekin}
  \item \emph{Recall:} \emph{mainū̃ nahī̃ patā} — from two chapters back
\end{itemize}

You have owned that first pair since page one and have never been told which to choose.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
Both pairs are the same shape, and it runs through the whole language:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਧੰਨਵਾਦ}} · \textbf{\pa{ਪਰ}} — the \textbf{inherited and Sanskritic} side
  \item \textbf{\pa{ਸ਼ੁਕਰੀਆ}} · \textbf{\pa{ਲੇਕਿਨ}} — the \textbf{Perso-Arabic} side
\end{itemize}

Punjabi has drawn on both streams for centuries, so a great many everyday ideas have two perfectly good words. What the choice carries:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item The Sanskritic word leans \textbf{formal and written}, and is the one you will most often see in print and hear in institutional or Sikh religious settings.
  \item The Perso-Arabic word leans \textbf{everyday and spoken}, and is more usual in Pakistani Punjabi and in Muslim communities.
  \item \textbf{Both are understood everywhere by everyone.} Choosing the other one is never an error, and it is never taken as one.
\end{itemize}

So this is not a rule about correctness. It is a rule about \textbf{what your choice tells the listener} — which is the same thing \textbf{\pa{ਤੂੰ}} against \textbf{\pa{ਤੁਸੀਂ}} told them, and the same thing the book's three greetings told them.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} thank a stranger at a counter, then a friend. Choose each time.
  \item \emph{Contrast:} \emph{par} and \emph{lekin} — which side of the pair is each on?
  \item \emph{Say it:} both members of both pairs, in two columns, aloud.
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Name both pairs and say which side each word is on. Is one member of a pair more correct than the other? (No — the choice tells the listener something; it does not make you right or wrong.)
\end{tcolorbox}
